title: Lovesac Rebounds on Tariff Refunds, Canada Fires Back Hard
subtitle: Trade escalation and soft builder confidence collide with a mattress industry asking whether procrastination, not the economy, is the real competitor.

content.title: Lovesac Rebounds on Tariff Refunds, Canada Fires Back Hard
content.subtitle: Trade escalation and soft builder confidence collide with a mattress industry asking whether procrastination, not the economy, is the real competitor.
content.greeting: Good morning. Lovesac turned a year-ago loss into a profit on the back of $21 million in tariff refunds, proof that trade policy is now a line item on the income statement, not just a talking point. Canada answered U.S. tariffs with retaliatory duties of up to 50% on $20 billion in goods, adding fresh cost pressure just as builder confidence slid to its lowest mark in a year. Furniture Today's Sheila Long O'Mara asks the harder question underneath all of it: with consumers still spending elsewhere, is the industry's real rival simply the decision to wait. Add Wayfair's Monday Night Football debut and a wave of K-beauty at Target, and the throughline is clear: brands are fighting for attention and dollars that haven't disappeared, just gone elsewhere.

top_stories.headline: Lovesac Swings to Profit on $21 Million in Tariff Refunds
top_stories.summary: Lovesac (NASDAQ: LOVE) posted Q2 FY2027 net sales of $161.2 million, up 0.4% year over year, with gross profit up 21.7% to $110.3 million. Net income hit $7.4 million, or 51 cents per diluted share, reversing a $6.7 million loss a year ago, largely on $21 million in IEEPA tariff refunds. CEO Shawn Nelson credited high-end configuration and add-ons like Reclining Seat and Storage for resilience against a choppy category backdrop. Full-year guidance calls for sales of $690 million to $710 million, but Q3 guidance projects a net loss of $9 million to $12 million. Retailers watching Lovesac's margin story should note how much of the swing came from trade policy rather than demand, a distinction worth making with any vendor citing tariff relief as a pricing tailwind.

top_stories.headline: Canada Hits Back With Tariffs Up to 50% on U.S. Goods
top_stories.summary: Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on roughly $20 billion in U.S. goods, including steel, aluminum, household appliances and forestry products, after bilateral trade talks collapsed. The measures mirror the value of Canadian goods hit by U.S. tariffs last month and double Canada's duties on American steel and aluminum. Prime Minister Mark Carney framed the response as matching the U.S. dollar for dollar rather than raising revenue. For furniture, the direct exposure runs through steel, aluminum, forestry products and appliances, all inputs into case goods, hardware and delivery equipment. Sourcing teams should press suppliers now on whether Canadian-linked inputs carry new cost, before it shows up unannounced in Q4 invoices.

top_stories.headline: Builder Confidence Hits a One Year Low as Fed Hikes Rates
top_stories.summary: The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell three points to 32 in September, its lowest level in a year, as the Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023. Thirty-eight percent of builders cut prices this month and 66% used sales incentives, both up from August. New home sales in July totaled 607,000, down 6.3% from a year earlier, and existing-home sales fell 1.7% in July to 4.06 million. Furniture sales track closely with home sales, since new floor plans and new bedrooms drive purchases. Retailers in markets with heavy new construction should expect a softer pipeline of move-in-driven big-ticket sales into year-end and lean harder on replacement and remodel messaging.

top_stories.headline: Mattress Industry's Real Rival May Be Procrastination, Not the Economy
top_stories.summary: Furniture Today's Sheila Long O'Mara lays out the data behind the industry's favorite excuses: Consumer Confidence Index down to 89.4 in August, Michigan sentiment down 13.2% year over year, mattress unit shipments off 13.2% in 2025 per the International Sleep Products Association. But July retail and food service sales were still up 5% year over year, showing consumers are spending, just not on mattresses, since a worn-out one can always wait another year. The practical read for sales floors: a considered, postponable purchase needs a specific reason to happen now, not a wait for confidence or rates to improve. Retailers should arm associates with a concrete health-and-wellness case for buying today, not a general pitch about comfort.

top_stories.headline: Storefronts Need to Be Legible to AI Shopping Agents
top_stories.summary: New guidance argues retailers should structure product data and site architecture so AI shopping agents can find, understand and transact with a storefront, treating agentic traffic as a new channel rather than a threat. The excerpt frames this as a near-term retail imperative rather than a distant trend. For furniture and mattress retailers, that means clean, structured SKU data covering dimensions, materials, price and availability, the same discipline that underpins any endless-aisle or marketplace strategy. With online share of home furnishings estimated well into the 30% range depending on the source, an independent retailer whose product feed isn't machine-readable is invisible to a growing slice of shoppers before a human ever sees the listing.

industry_moves.headline: Liberty Furniture Names New Senior VP of Sales
industry_moves.summary: Liberty Furniture has appointed a new senior vice president of sales, according to a Furniture Today report. Details on the executive's background and mandate were not available beyond the announcement itself. Leadership changes in sales leadership typically signal a company sharpening its go-to-market push heading into fourth-quarter and spring market planning. Retail buyers working with Liberty should expect outreach to introduce the new leader and confirm program continuity in the months ahead.

industry_moves.headline: MotoMotion Dangles Equity to Retain Staff Through Tariff Squeeze
industry_moves.summary: MotoMotion China has proposed granting roughly 3 million shares, about 1% of the company, to its board, middle managers and U.S.-based managers, costing about $7 million in compensation over five years. The filing candidly cites a Chinese furniture industry where profits have fallen more than 52% on soft U.S. demand, tariffs and currency headwinds. More than 90% of the shares go to a 180-person pool of midlevel staff, not top executives, signaling a retention play rather than an executive reward. Shareholders vote Oct. 9. It is a rare public acknowledgment from a supplier of just how much tariff pressure is squeezing margins upstream.

industry_moves.headline: Lifestyle Enterprise Marks 30 Years With 30-Plus Factories
industry_moves.summary: Lifestyle Enterprise is celebrating its 30th anniversary now working with more than 30 factories and raw-material suppliers and over 130 sourcing employees worldwide. CEO Michael Hsieh, son of founder William Hsieh, has expanded the sourcing firm beyond core case goods and upholstery into massage chairs, cabinet beds and sound-integrated furniture. The anniversary underscores how far sourcing intermediaries have scaled diversification as a hedge against tariff and demand volatility. Retailers sourcing through Lifestyle should ask how the expanded category mix, particularly tech-driven furniture, can differentiate a floor set for spring.

retail_trends.headline: Target Bets on K-Beauty to Reset Its Beauty Business
retail_trends.summary: Target's new Beauty Studio replaces former in-store Ulta shops with more than 1,600 products from 90 brands, adding six K-beauty favorites and quadrupling its Korean beauty assortment this year. The move mirrors Ulta and Sephora both expanding K-beauty lines, signaling Korean brands' move from specialty retail into mass channels. For home furnishings, the lesson is about assortment refresh as a growth lever: Target is using a trending category to re-earn foot traffic and reset its financial trajectory, a strategy furniture retailers can apply with trending categories like wellness or outdoor.

retail_trends.headline: Rothy's Growth Discipline Offers a DTC Survival Playbook
retail_trends.summary: Rothy's, which crossed $211 million in sales last year, has stayed profitable while DTC peers like Allbirds struggled, according to CEO Dayna Quanbeck on the Modern Retail Podcast. Her stated challenge now is avoiding distraction from growth and expanding physical retail only at a sustainable pace rather than chasing scale. For furniture DTC brands testing showrooms, the takeaway is the same discipline: floor samples paired with a controlled footprint beat rapid store expansion that outpaces fulfillment and cash flow.

retail_trends.headline: Beyond Credit Union Signals Retailers Chasing Financial Services
retail_trends.summary: Neighborhood Intelligence, formerly Bed Bath & Beyond, is launching Beyond Credit Union with Alliant Credit Union in the first quarter of next year, covering checking, savings, credit cards and home equity products. CEO Marcus Lemonis pitched it as helping customers manage the cost of homeownership more intelligently. For furniture retailers already competing on financing terms for big-ticket purchases, a home-focused brand entering banking is a reminder that the credit relationship, not just the sale, is becoming a retention tool worth owning or partnering on.

supply_chain.headline: Canada's $20 Billion Tariff Package Targets Steel, Appliances
supply_chain.summary: Canada's new tariffs, effective at 12:01 a.m. Tuesday, range from 15% to 50% and cover steel, aluminum, household appliances, dairy and electronics, matching the value of U.S. duties imposed after talks collapsed Aug. 21. Economists cited by CBS flagged Midwestern manufacturers as especially exposed. Furniture Today notes the tariffs add to uncertainty around USMCA's future, a pact underpinning integrated North American supply chains. Sourcing and logistics teams should map any Canadian-linked components, from appliances to hardware, and confirm with vendors whether costs will be absorbed or passed through before Q4 orders lock in.

supply_chain.headline: Freight Costs, Not Just Tariffs, Are Squeezing Q4 Margins
supply_chain.summary: Beyond tariffs, fallout from the Iran conflict is pushing ocean freight costs higher, with East Coast spot rates near $9,000 per 40-foot container in mid-August and West Coast rates up 11% week over week to around $6,800, per Furniture Today's Bill McLoughlin. Canada is the fourth-largest furniture exporter to the U.S. at $1.2 billion and the top buyer of U.S. furniture at $1.4 billion, making the trade dispute doubly disruptive. Haverty's CEO Steve Burdette cited a 25% to 30% jump in container rates from bunker fuel surcharges. Retailers should expect vendor price increases tied to freight, not just duties, heading into the fourth quarter and should ask suppliers to separate the two on any cost justification.

ai_tech.headline: Wayfair Goes to Monday Night Football With New Brand Platform
ai_tech.summary: Wayfair debuted "Wayfair Delivers," a brand platform built around delivery and trust, with an ad featuring NFL quarterback Matthew Stafford and his family airing during Monday Night Football on ESPN and ABC. The company is increasing football-related ad spend to five times its previous level and highlighting Wayfair Verified, Wayfair Rewards and its logistics network. For independent retailers, it is a reminder that the largest online furniture player is spending heavily to own the delivery and trust narrative, the same territory where a local retailer's white-glove service could compete if marketed as aggressively.

ai_tech.headline: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra Pressures Anthropic Ahead of IPO
ai_tech.summary: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra has captured about 13% of enterprise AI spending tracked by Ramp versus roughly 8% for Anthropic's Claude Fable, and OpenRouter reports users spent more on OpenAI models last week for the first time in over two years. Anthropic is weighing a new model release ahead of an expected IPO, even after CEO Dario Amodei called for an industrywide safety slowdown. For furniture retailers building AI tools into product search or customer service, the competitive scramble between model providers means today's vendor choice may not be tomorrow's leader, so contracts should stay flexible on model swaps.

ai_tech.headline: Anthropic Publishes Metrics on AI Building Its Own Successors
ai_tech.summary: Anthropic disclosed that Claude models are involved in roughly 26% of the work building the company's next generation of AI, part of a new transparency effort to track how much AI development is becoming self-directed. The company plans to embed independent evaluators to verify safety practices as the pace of AI capability gains accelerates. For furniture operators adopting AI tools for merchandising or customer service, the pace of underlying model change is a planning risk: tools bought today may be built differently, and faster, than vendors currently describe.

one_thing.headline: Give Shoppers a Reason to Buy Now
one_thing.body: Consumer sentiment is down and mattress unit shipments fell 13.2% in 2025, but retail sales are still up 5% year over year. The gap is procrastination, not empty wallets. This week, audit sales scripts and product data alike: make sure associates have a specific, health-based reason to buy today, and make sure that same product story is structured cleanly enough for online shoppers and AI agents to find it without a salesperson in the room.

content.closing: Tomorrow's Brief will track how Canada's tariffs move through vendor pricing, more Q2 earnings commentary on freight costs, and further AI shopping tool launches ahead of the holiday season.
